title: A partner
hookLine: a chavruta for the long run
tomorrow: same book every year: is the weekly portion a rerun?

cards: A running partner texts at six in the morning: you up? And somehow you go, on a morning you'd have skipped alone. The Talmud has a strange line about people who skip the partner.
It takes a verse from Jeremiah about a sword coming against the boasters, and reads it as a sword against scholars who sit and study by themselves. A sword? For reading alone?

teach.b: The answer is a pun. The Hebrew word in the verse, baddim, sounds like bad, alone. So the Talmud says: a sword on those who study alone, and worse, they grow foolish.
Because alone, nobody pushes back. You read a line, decide what it means, and nobody says: wait, look again. The same page gives the other side.
Proverbs says, "Iron sharpeneth iron," and the Talmud reads it as two scholars sharpening each other. That's a chavruta: a study partner. Two people, one text, reading out loud, asking, arguing.
Often noisy. And here's the story to tell a friend tonight. The Talmud tells of Choni, who slept so long that when he woke and walked into the study house, nobody believed who he was.
Alone and unrecognized, he was miserable, and the Talmud sums it up with a saying: either a study partner, or death.
A partner for the long run isn't someone who knows more than you. It's someone who shows up, reads the line beside you, and says what they really think, especially when it isn't what you think.

how: Traditional Jewish study is often done in chavruta, two partners reading a text aloud together, questioning and arguing; study halls are known for the noise of many pairs at once.

o: a tutor who explains the hard parts for you
a study partner who reads beside you and pushes back
a sponsor who pays for someone's study

games.q: a sword, a pun, a partner — tap the pairs.

s: the Talmud's 'sword' line is about study, read through a pun
baddim, boasters, sounds like bad, alone.
a chavruta is a teacher who explains the text to you
a partner reads beside you, and you sharpen each other.
the Talmud praises studying alone as the purest kind
it warns that those who study alone can grow foolish; iron sharpens iron.

games.q: you've been reading Psalms alone every night and you're sure you get them. a friend offers to read with you, but you'd rather not argue. what does the Talmud's pun warn?
o: alone, nobody pushes back, and you can fool yourself.
studying alone is forbidden outright, so stop tonight.
reading Psalms alone doesn't count as real study.
games.why: the Talmud reads baddim as 'alone' and warns that solo learners grow foolish. two scholars sharpen each other, like iron on iron.

practice: Think of one person who'd be good to learn with: a friend, a parent, a grandparent, anyone who asks good questions. Write them a message inviting them to read one short text with you this week, and name the text.
Send it now, or keep it ready for when it feels right.

wordCard.voice: A partner: a chavruta, someone who reads the same text beside you for the long run, and pushes back.

carryVoice: Your line: learn in pairs. Iron sharpens iron, and nobody sharpens alone. That's it for today.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 7a (Jeremiah 50:36 'a sword upon the baddim' read as scholars who study alone, who grow foolish; Proverbs 27:17 read as two scholars sharpening each other)
Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 23a (Choni wakes, is not recognized in the study house; 'either companionship or death')
